questions.question: Is there really a secret Treasury account in my name that can pay off my debts?

central.text: The evidence does not support "You can draw on a secret Treasury account to pay debts by writing "accepted for value" on bills"

questions.premise: The redemption story runs in three steps: the government created a strawman in your all-caps name, sold your birth certificate as a bond, and holds the proceeds in a Treasury account you can draw on by writing 'accepted for value'. Treasury says the account does not exist and the birth certificate has no monetary value; courts in the US, Canada and Australia have called the strawman a myth and the instruments worthless. On the cost, the fraud convictions in the record are of promoters and of people who passed the bills, and a homeowner who paid her mortgage with one lost the house; the sources do not count how often ordinary users are prosecuted, and one cites tax-filing fraud cases rather than debt instruments.
questions.tension: The story links a real document (your birth certificate) to a real agency (the Treasury), so each step sounds checkable, but no step exists.
questions.whyWatch: The redemption story promises debts paid from an account you never knew you had; Treasury, the IRS and the courts say what happens to the people who try it.

arc.hook: A homeowner sends her bank a $244,663 bill of exchange drawn on her secret Treasury account.
arc.conflict: Each step of the story points to something real, a birth certificate, the Treasury, the commercial code, and promoters sell the kit that ties them together.
arc.evidence: Treasury and the IRS on the account and the instruments; courts on the strawman (Gravatt, Queensland, Canada); Bryant v. Washington Mutual on what the bill of exchange was worth.
arc.resolution: No account, no bond, no strawman: the instruments are worthless in every ruling here. Prosecution is real for promoters and those who passed the bills; how often ordinary users are charged is not measured.
arc.takeaway: If a payment method needs you to believe the Treasury is hiding your money, the bank will treat it as no payment.

questions.question: But since the US left gold in 1933, isn't money just credit, so a debt can only be discharged, never paid?

central.text: Contrary to the sources that repeat it, the evidence does not support "Since the 1933 gold suspension, money is credit and debts cannot be lawfully paid, only discharged"

questions.premise: The claim reads the 1933 move off gold as turning money into credit, so debts can only be discharged, never paid. A federal court read the 1933 joint resolution itself and found it makes US currency legal tender for all debts, saying nothing about discharge; Congress declares Federal Reserve Notes legal tender, and federal circuits reject as frivolous the claim that they are merely debts.
questions.tension: The claim cites a real 1933 law, and the US really did leave the gold standard, yet the law says the opposite of what the claim needs.
questions.whyWatch: The 1933 story is the foundation the redemption kits stand on; reading the resolution itself shows what it did and did not do.

arc.hook: The redemption kits all start in 1933, when the US stopped paying in gold.
arc.conflict: The claim says that from then on money is only credit, so a debt can be discharged but never paid.
arc.evidence: House Joint Resolution 192 as Bryant v. Washington Mutual reads it; 31 USC 5103 and the circuit rulings the IRS collects on Federal Reserve Notes.
arc.resolution: The resolution made US currency legal tender for all debts, dollar for dollar; paying in Federal Reserve Notes is lawful payment.
arc.takeaway: Leaving gold changed what a dollar is backed by, not whether it pays a debt.
